entities.rationale: ExistenceNecessitation already models the disposition of a substance to exist necessarily (causa sui entails necessary existence). This individual is the specific token of that disposition inhering in God, complementing the quality.

entities.label: InfinitudeOfSubstance
entities.rationale: Spinoza's claim that Substance is necessarily infinite is best modeled as a disposition (internally grounded realizable) inhering in Substance. It expresses the intrinsic, necessary capacity/nature of Substance to be infinite — not an externally assigned role. It is an individual disposition instance inhering in the individual God/Substance.

relations.rationale: InfinitudeOfSubstance is an instance of Disposition (BFO_0000016), an internally grounded realizable entity.
The disposition of necessary infinitude inheres in God (the individual Substance). BFO requires that specifically dependent continuants inhere in their bearers.

Necessary infinitude is closely related to ExistenceNecessitation (the internally grounded capacity by which Substance necessarily exists/is). However, this is a relation between the instance and the class hierarchy — more precisely the instance type should be linked. Flagging in open_questions instead.

open_questions: Should InfinitudeOfSubstance be typed as a subclass of ExistenceNecessitation (i.e., is infinite existence a species of existence-necessitation), or is it a distinct disposition alongside ExistenceNecessitation? The existing individual NecessaryExistenceOfGod already captures necessary existence; should InfinitudeOfSubstance be related to it via some parthood or is it a distinct claim?

The statement 'Substance is necessarily infinite' — does 'infinite' here mean infinite in all attributes (absolute infinity, already captured by AbsoluteInfinity quality on God), or infinite in its own kind/attribute? If the former, should we simply link the existing AbsoluteInfinity quality to Substance rather than minting a new disposition?

Should the necessity of infinitude be modeled as a disposition (internally grounded, as proposed) or as a quality (AbsoluteInfinity already exists as BFO_0000019 quality on God)? If AbsoluteInfinity already captures this, no new entity may be needed.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that Substance (identified with God in the ontology) is necessarily infinite. Two existing individuals are relevant: AbsoluteInfinity (a Quality individual of type BFO_0000019 already in the graph) and NecessaryExistenceOfGod (a Disposition individual of type BFO_0000016). The 'necessarily infinite' claim has two components: (1) the quality of being infinite (already partially captured by AbsoluteInfinity) and (2) the modal necessity of that infinitude (analogous to NecessaryExistenceOfGod). Rather than duplicate, I propose a new disposition individual InfinitudeOfSubstance to capture the necessary-infinitude specifically, inhering in God. The third relation I tentatively propose — linking it as a subclass of ExistenceNecessitation — is actually a class-level assertion that may not apply to an individual; I flag this in open_questions. The user should confirm whether AbsoluteInfinity already suffices and no new entity is needed, or whether the modal necessity dimension warrants a separate disposition.

proposal.utterance: Only one substance exists.

entities.label: SubstanceUniquenessConstraint
entities.rationale: The proposition 'only one substance exists' is a propositional content — an information artifact or doctrinal claim that can be entertained, copied, and referred to. BFO_0000031 (generically dependent continuant) best captures propositional/informational content. It inheres in TheEthics as its bearer (the work in which it is asserted).

entities.label: SubstanceNumericalUniquenessQuality
entities.rationale: The property of being the only one — numerical uniqueness — is a quality that inheres in the individual God/WholeOfNature (the sole substance). Modeling it as a Quality (BFO_0000019) on that bearer captures the ontological commitment that there is exactly one such entity.

relations.rationale: The uniqueness claim is part of the content of TheEthics, where Spinoza explicitly argues for monism.
Numerical uniqueness (being the sole substance) inheres in God/the one substance as its bearer, per Spinoza's monism.
Spinoza's claim entails that God is the unique instance of Substance; typing God as a Substance individual makes the monism claim formally expressible.

open_questions: Should God and WholeOfNature be asserted to be identical (owl:sameAs), since both have been typed as BFO_0000004 independent continuants representing the single substance?
Should SubstanceNumericalUniquenessQuality also inheres in WholeOfNature, or is WholeOfNature already equated with God for this purpose?
Do you want a cardinality axiom (owl:maxCardinality 1 on Substance) to formally enforce monism in the reasoner?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'Only one substance exists' asserts Spinoza's metaphysical monism. Ontologically this involves two commitments: (1) a propositional/doctrinal content — the uniqueness claim itself — which is a generically dependent continuant (BFO_0000031) that is part of TheEthics; and (2) a quality of numerical uniqueness that inheres in the sole substance, God. I reuse the existing individual God (already typed BFO_0000004) and the existing class Substance. A new individual SubstanceNumericalUniquenessQuality (BFO_0000019) inheres in God, and a new individual SubstanceUniquenessConstraint (BFO_0000031) is part of TheEthics. I also add rdf:type working:Substance to God to make the monism claim tractable to a reasoner. Open questions flag the owl:sameAs issue with WholeOfNature and whether a cardinality axiom is desired.

proposal.utterance: Thinking and Extended are two infinite Attributes of Substance.

entities.label: Thinking
entities.rationale: Thinking (Cogitatio) is one of the infinite Attributes of Substance in Spinoza's system. Attributes inhere in Substance as qualities through which the intellect perceives Substance's essence. It is an individual instance of DivineAttribute (itself a subclass of BFO Quality).

entities.label: Extension
entities.rationale: Extension (Extensio) is the other paradigmatic infinite Attribute of Substance. Like Thinking, it is an individual instance of DivineAttribute, inhering in Substance.

entities.label: God_SubstanceIndividual
entities.rationale: Reusing existing individual working:God. The utterance identifies Substance with God/Nature (already established). Adding rdf:type working:Substance to make the typing explicit.

relations.rationale: Thinking is an instance of the DivineAttribute class.
Extension is an instance of the DivineAttribute class.
The Attribute Thinking inheres in Substance (God), per BFO's inheres-in relation for specifically dependent continuants.
The Attribute Extension inheres in Substance (God), per BFO's inheres-in relation.
The utterance identifies the bearer of these Attributes as Substance; God is already typed BFO_0000004 and should also be typed working:Substance to reflect the ontological commitment.

open_questions: Spinoza holds there are infinitely many Attributes, of which only Thinking and Extension are known to human minds. Should we represent this as a cardinality constraint or an open-world assumption on DivineAttribute instances?

DivineAttribute is currently a subclass of BFO Quality (BFO_0000019). Spinoza's Attributes are defined as 'what the intellect perceives as constituting the essence of Substance.' This has an epistemic dimension that Quality alone may not capture. Should we also type DivineAttribute as a subclass of BFO_0000031 (Generically dependent continuant) to capture the representational/conceptual aspect, or keep it purely as Quality?
Should 'Thinking' and 'Extension' also bear an 'infinite' quality (perhaps a new InfinityQuality individual) to capture that they are *infinite* Attributes as stated in the utterance?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts two specific infinite Attributes of Substance: Thinking (Cogitatio) and Extension (Extensio). In Spinoza's Ethics, Attributes are what the intellect perceives as constituting the essence of Substance; in BFO terms, the closest fit is that they are specifically dependent continuants (Qualities) inhering in their unique bearer, Substance (God). Both are minted as new individuals of the existing class DivineAttribute (subclass of BFO_0000019 Quality) and linked to the existing individual God via RO_0000052 (inheres in). God is additionally typed as working:Substance to make explicit that the bearer referred to in 'Substance' is the same individual. The open questions flag potential refinements around the infinite cardinality of Attributes, their epistemic-representational character, and whether an explicit infinity quality should be attached.

proposal.utterance: Finite singular things are modes of Substance's attributes.

entities.label: FiniteSingularThing
entities.rationale: Finite singular things are particular, bounded existents in Spinoza's system — they are independent continuants (not merely qualities or dispositions), and typing them as a subclass of BFO_0000004 is consistent with Substance already being BFO_0000004. They are not modes in the BFO sense but in Spinoza's sense they are modifications; see relation below.

entities.label: AttributeOfSubstance
entities.rationale: In Spinoza an Attribute is what intellect perceives as constituting the essence of Substance — a fundamental, irreducible quality-dimension (e.g. Extension, Thought). Modeling as a subclass of Quality (BFO_0000019) captures its character as a property that inheres in Substance while being ontologically real. Already DivineAttribute exists as BFO_0000019; AttributeOfSubstance is a more general class of which DivineAttribute can be a subclass.

entities.label: SpinozisticMode
entities.rationale: Spinoza's 'mode' is an affection of Substance that exists in and is conceived through another (Ethics 1D5). This maps onto BFO specifically dependent continuant: it inheres in a bearer (the Attribute / Substance) and cannot exist independently. The existing working:Mode class already captures this; SpinozisticMode is explicitly identified as the class of finite singular things' modal character. We can make FiniteSingularThing bear a SpinozisticMode instance, or subclass Mode directly.

entities.label: FiniteSingularThingModeInstance
entities.rationale: The assertion says finite singular things ARE modes — i.e., each finite singular thing instantiates a mode of an attribute. We model this as a subclass of ModeInstance that inheres in an AttributeOfSubstance bearer, distinguishing modes that are finite and singular from infinite modes.

relations.rationale: DivineAttribute (already in ontology) is the specific case where the attribute belongs to God/Substance; AttributeOfSubstance is the more general class.
Finite-singular-thing modes are a species of ModeInstance.
Each FiniteSingularThingModeInstance inheres in (RO_0000052) an AttributeOfSubstance as its bearer, capturing Spinoza's claim that modes exist 'in' and are 'conceived through' an attribute.

A finite singular thing (as independent continuant) is the bearer of a FiniteSingularThingModeInstance — i.e., it bears a modal character that is its existence as a modification of Substance's attribute.
Finite singular things are independent continuants.
Finitude (already in ontology as BFO_0000019 quality) inheres in finite singular things as their defining quality of being bounded/limited.
FiniteThingRole (already in ontology as BFO_0000023) inheres in finite singular things, marking their relational/functional status as finite entities within the modal system.

open_questions: Should FiniteSingularThing be modeled as a subclass of BFO_0000004 (independent continuant) or should it be typed instead as a bearer of a Mode (i.e., should 'finite singular thing' just BE the mode/SDC itself, as Spinoza implies)? The tension is that Spinoza identifies the singular thing with the mode, but BFO separates bearers from their dependent continuants.
Do you want to distinguish finite modes from infinite modes at this stage (e.g., infinite immediate modes like motion-and-rest, and infinite mediate modes, versus finite singular things)?

Should AttributeOfSubstance remain a quality class, or would you prefer it modeled as a generically dependent continuant (BFO_0000031), given that some interpreters treat attributes as conceptual structures rather than real qualities of Substance?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts Spinoza's Ethics 1D5/1P25C thesis: finite singular things (res particulares finitae) are modes of Substance's attributes. We introduce: (1) FiniteSingularThing as a new class (subclass of BFO_0000004, independent continuant) since finite things persist and have causal identity in Spinoza; (2) AttributeOfSubstance as a new class (subclass of BFO_0000019, quality) of which the existing DivineAttribute is a subclass; (3) FiniteSingularThingModeInstance as a subclass of the existing ModeInstance, typed as BFO_0000020 (specifically dependent continuant), inhering in an AttributeOfSubstance. The relation of 'being a mode of an attribute' is captured via RO_0000052 (inheres in) from FiniteSingularThingModeInstance to AttributeOfSubstance, and RO_0000053 (bearer of) from FiniteSingularThing to FiniteSingularThingModeInstance. The existing Finitude quality and FiniteThingRole are linked to FiniteSingularThing. A key BFO modeling challenge is flagged: Spinoza identifies finite things with their modal being, whereas BFO requires a bearer distinct from its dependent properties; the chosen solution maintains a bearer-mode distinction and notes this in open_questions.

proposal.utterance: God is an immanent cause of all things.

entities.label: ImmanentCausation
entities.rationale: Immanent causation is an internally-grounded causal capacity of God/Substance — it is not externally assigned but flows from the nature of the substance itself, making Disposition the best BFO fit. It is a class because it names a kind of causal disposition.

entities.label: GodImmanentCauseRole
entities.rationale: The specific role-instance by which God (the individual) bears the immanent cause relation to all things. Modeled as an individual role instance inhering in the God individual, of type ImmanentCausation (which is a subclass of Disposition). Note: in Spinoza immanent causation is arguably intrinsic, but as a role it captures the relational dimension toward created things.

entities.label: AllThings
entities.rationale: The totality of finite modes/things caused by God. This maps closely to the existing WholeOfNature individual; reuse is preferred — see open_questions.

entities.label: ImmanentCausationProcess
entities.rationale: The ongoing process by which God immanently causes all things — God acts through, not outside, the things caused. A process class distinct from DeterminingRelation (which captures logical determination between modes).

relations.rationale: The individual role instance is typed as ImmanentCausation disposition.
God (the individual Substance) bears the immanent cause disposition/role.
Inverse: the role inheres in God.
The immanent cause disposition is realized in the immanent causation process (God causing all things).
The immanent causation process has God as a participant (as cause).
The immanent causation process has the totality of things (WholeOfNature) as participant (as effect/product).
ImmanentCausation is a subclass of BFO Disposition.
ImmanentCausationProcess is a subclass of BFO Process.

The existing GodFirstCauseRole individual's type (BFO_0000023 Role) is compatible with ImmanentCausation only if we treat first-cause as a distinct role; flagged in open_questions. Left as a tentative subtype suggestion.

open_questions: Should 'AllThings' be identified with the existing working:WholeOfNature individual, or is a distinct individual needed (e.g., WholeOfNature is Natura Naturata, while AllThings may include both modes and attributes)?
Spinoza distinguishes immanent causation from transient causation (Eth. I P18). Should we add a class TransientCausation as a sibling of ImmanentCausation under Disposition for completeness?

The existing working:GodFirstCauseRole individual is typed BFO_0000023 (Role). Should it be re-typed or subsumed under ImmanentCausation (Disposition), or kept separate because 'first cause' and 'immanent cause' are distinct aspects of God's causality in Spinoza?

Is ImmanentCausation better modeled as a Disposition (internally grounded in God's nature) or as a Role (relationally defined with respect to finite things)? Spinoza's text supports Disposition (it follows from God's essence), but the relational aspect to 'all things' suggests a dual characterization.

Should we assert that working:NaturaNaturans is the participant in ImmanentCausationProcess rather than working:God directly, since Natura Naturans is Spinoza's technical term for God as active cause?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'God is an immanent cause of all things' asserts a core Spinozistic causal thesis (Ethics I P18). I model this by introducing: (1) a new class ImmanentCausation as a BFO Disposition (internally grounded in God's infinite nature), (2) an individual GodImmanentCauseRole of that type inhering in the existing God individual via RO_0000052/RO_0000053, (3) a new process class ImmanentCausationProcess (BFO Process) in which the disposition is realized, having both God and WholeOfNature as participants. I reuse the existing working:WholeOfNature individual for 'all things', pending clarification. The existing working:GodFirstCauseRole individual is noted as potentially overlapping but kept distinct pending user confirmation. Several open questions are raised about the precise ontological category of immanent causation and the relationship to NaturaNaturans.

proposal.utterance: God necessarily causes all things.

entities.label: GodCausesAllThings
entities.rationale: The necessity by which God causes all things is an internally grounded causal power inhering in God (Substance). It is best typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) because it is an intrinsic, necessary capacity that flows from God's essence. It is related to but distinct from CausaSui (self-causation); it is the outward-facing causal necessity. It could also be a Quality, but since it is a productive power it fits Disposition better.

entities.label: GodCausesAllThingsProcess
entities.rationale: The actual causing of all things by God is an occurrent — a Process in BFO. It is the realization of GodCausesAllThings (the disposition). It is a subtype of DeterminingRelation (already a Process class in the ontology), since God's necessary causation is a determining process over all finite things.

relations.rationale: The disposition GodCausesAllThings inheres in God (the Substance individual), per BFO's 'inheres in' relation for specifically dependent continuants.
God is the bearer of the disposition GodCausesAllThings.
The disposition is realized in the process of God's necessary causation of all things.
The process realizes the disposition (inverse of realized in).
God participates in the process of causing all things as the primary agent/participant.
God's necessary causation of all things is part of God's necessary existence disposition — the two are closely related as aspects of divine necessity in Spinoza's system.

open_questions: Should 'all things' (WholeOfNature / NaturaNaturans) be explicitly represented as the output or patient of GodCausesAllThingsProcess? If so, should working:WholeOfNature or working:NaturaNaturans participate in the process?

proposal.utterance: Nature possesses a striving to preserve its state and being.

entities.label: Conatus
entities.rationale: Spinoza's conatus is the intrinsic striving of a thing to persevere in its own being. It is internally grounded (not externally conferred), making it a Disposition in BFO terms. It is a kind (common noun), so it is a class. It applies to Nature/WholeOfNature and all finite things.

entities.label: ConatusOfNature
entities.rationale: The specific conatus instance inhering in WholeOfNature (Spinoza's whole of Nature / God) — the striving of Nature to preserve its state and being. This is an individual disposition inhering in the individual WholeOfNature.

relations.rationale: ConatusOfNature is an instance of the Conatus class.
The disposition (conatus) inheres in its bearer, WholeOfNature, per BFO's inheres-in relation.
WholeOfNature is the bearer of ConatusOfNature (inverse of inheres-in).
Conatus is a subclass of BFO Disposition, being an internally grounded striving.

open_questions: Should Conatus also apply to FiniteSingularThing instances (Spinoza holds every finite thing also has a conatus), or is this utterance restricted to Nature as a whole?

Is the 'state' (status) being preserved best modeled as a Quality or as participation in a Process — Spinoza sometimes speaks of it as 'esse' (being), suggesting EssentialExistenceQuality already in the ontology could be related?

Should ConatusOfNature be linked to NecessaryExistenceOfGod or GodNecessaryExistenceDisposition as a related or sub-disposition, given that God/Nature's self-preservation is grounded in its necessary existence?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that Nature has an intrinsic striving to preserve its own state and being — Spinoza's conatus doctrine. This is best modeled as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) because it is internally grounded in the bearer's own nature rather than externally conferred. I introduce a new class Conatus (subclass of Disposition) and an individual ConatusOfNature as the specific disposition inhering in the existing individual WholeOfNature. proposal.utterance: All contingency is excluded from the universe.

entities.label: AbsenceOfContingency
entities.rationale: The absence of contingency across the whole of nature/universe is a quality borne by the WholeOfNature individual — it is a specific, measurable (or logically determinable) property of that entity in Spinoza's system, asserting that everything is necessarily determined.

entities.label: UniversalNecessityDisposition
entities.rationale: The universe (WholeOfNature) has an internally grounded disposition toward universal necessity — i.e., it is disposed such that every thing in it is necessarily determined, leaving no room for contingency. This models the causal/dispositional ground of that quality.

relations.rationale: The quality of having no contingency inheres in the WholeOfNature individual, which represents the universe in Spinoza's system.
WholeOfNature is the bearer of the AbsenceOfContingency quality (inverse of inheres-in).
The disposition toward universal necessity inheres in the WholeOfNature individual as its internal ground.
WholeOfNature bears the UniversalNecessityDisposition (inverse of inheres-in).
The absence of contingency is an instance of EssentialExistenceQuality, linking it to the existing class that represents qualities tied to necessary existence in Spinoza's system.

open_questions: Should 'contingency' itself be modeled as a class (e.g., ContingencyQuality) so that AbsenceOfContingency can be formally defined as its negation or complement?

Is the bearer of this quality strictly the WholeOfNature individual, or should it also inhere in God (the Substance individual), given that God = WholeOfNature in Spinoza's system? Should we assert an identity or equivalence between God and WholeOfNature?
Should UniversalNecessityDisposition be related to the existing NecessaryExistenceOfGod or ExistenceNecessitation individuals/classes via a subclass or parthood relation?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts Spinoza's doctrine (Ethics Part I, Props 29–33) that everything in the universe is necessarily determined and that contingency is entirely excluded. Ontologically, this is best captured as a Quality inhering in the WholeOfNature individual (AbsenceOfContingency) and a Disposition that is its internal ground (UniversalNecessityDisposition). Both inhere in the existing WholeOfNature individual. The AbsenceOfContingency quality is typed as an instance of the existing EssentialExistenceQuality class, connecting it to the broader necessity-of-existence cluster already in the ontology. No new classes are strictly required, though an optional ContingencyQuality class could make the negation explicit. Open questions flag the God/WholeOfNature identity issue and possible linkage to existing necessity-related individuals.

proposal.utterance: Good and evil are beings of reason or modes of thinking.

entities.label: GoodAndEvil
entities.rationale: Spinoza treats 'good' and 'evil' as beings of reason (entia rationis) — cognitive or conceptual posits, not mind-independent features of reality. As beings of reason they are patterns of thought that can be instantiated in multiple minds, fitting BFO Generically Dependent Continuant. Making them a subclass of working:Idea (already GDC) captures their status as mental/conceptual content in Spinoza's system.

entities.label: BeingOfReason
entities.rationale: An ens rationis (being of reason) in Scholastic/Spinozistic usage is an entity that exists only in and through thought — a GDC that depends generically on cognizing minds. It is a supertype for both GoodAndEvil and ModeOfThinking in this context.

entities.label: ModeOfThinking
entities.rationale: Spinoza's 'modes of thinking' (modi cogitandi) — such as love, desire, good, evil — are modifications of the attribute of Thought. As cognitive/representational items that can be reproduced across minds, they are GDCs. Subclassing BeingOfReason captures the equating assertion in the utterance.

relations.rationale: The utterance asserts that good and evil are beings of reason; GoodAndEvil is therefore a subclass of BeingOfReason.
The utterance additionally identifies good and evil as modes of thinking, so GoodAndEvil is also a subclass of ModeOfThinking.
The utterance equates beings of reason with modes of thinking; ModeOfThinking is therefore a subclass (or co-extensive subtype) of BeingOfReason.

open_questions: Should GoodAndEvil be a class (for any instance of the concept) or a pair of individuals (for 'Good' and 'Evil' as specific Spinozistic entia rationis)? Splitting into working:Good and working:Evil as individuals of class BeingOfReason may be more precise.

Should ModeOfThinking be typed under working:Mode (already in the ontology as BFO_0000020 / SDC) rather than as a GDC? Spinoza's modes of thinking in the attribute-of-Thought sense inhere in a mind (SDC), but as beings of reason they are also shareable patterns (GDC). How should we resolve this tension?
Is this assertion drawn from a specific proposition in the Ethics (e.g., Ethics IV Preface) or from the Short Treatise? Knowing the source would help assign a PrimaryInterpretiveSourceRole.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance encodes a key Spinozistic metaphysical claim (cf. Ethics IV Preface, Short Treatise II): 'good' and 'evil' are not objective features of reality but entia rationis — beings that exist only insofar as minds conceive them — and are therefore modes of thinking (modi cogitandi). BFO-wise, items that exist only in thought and can be reproduced across cognizers map most naturally to Generically Dependent Continuant (BFO_0000031), consistent with the existing working:Idea class. I introduce three new classes: BeingOfReason (supertype, GDC, subclass of Idea), ModeOfThinking (equated with BeingOfReason by the utterance, GDC), and GoodAndEvil (subclass of both). The main open tension is whether ModeOfThinking should instead be an SDC (inhering in a specific mind), but the generically-dependent reading is more faithful to the claim that multiple minds can share the same concepts of good and evil.

proposal.utterance: Knowledge or perception occurs in humans in four kinds or ways.

entities.label: KnowledgeOrPerception
entities.rationale: Knowledge or perception in Spinoza is a capacity or disposition of a human mind/intellect to apprehend things. Typed as Disposition (BFO_0000016) since it is internally grounded in a bearer (the human intellect).

entities.label: KnowledgeKind
entities.rationale: The four 'kinds or ways' of knowledge are roles or modes that a knowledge-or-perception disposition can be realized in; externally classifiable kinds. Alternatively could be subtypes of KnowledgeOrPerception as dispositions. Marking as open question.

entities.label: Human
entities.rationale: Humans are material entities (persons with mass and spatial extent) that bear the knowledge/perception disposition. Spinoza's text explicitly localizes these four kinds in humans.

relations.rationale: KnowledgeOrPerception is a subclass of Disposition (BFO_0000016), internally grounded in the human intellect.
The four kinds/ways are subclasses of KnowledgeOrPerception, representing different modes or ways of knowing.
Human beings are material entities per BFO.
KnowledgeOrPerception inheres in Human as its bearer class, since knowledge is a disposition of human minds.

open_questions: Should the four 'kinds or ways' of knowledge be modeled as four subclasses of KnowledgeOrPerception (each a Disposition subtype), rather than as Roles? Spinoza in the TIE/Short Treatise distinguishes: (1) knowledge from hearsay/signs, (2) knowledge from vague experience, (3) knowledge from reason/demonstration, (4) intuitive knowledge. Should each of these four be minted as a named class now?

Is this utterance from the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect (TEI) or the Short Treatise? The TEI and Short Treatise present slightly different fourfold classifications; which text should this be attributed to?
Should 'Human' here be linked to the existing 'Intellect' individual/class already in the ontology, since knowledge inheres in Intellect specifically rather than the whole human body?

Is KnowledgeOrPerception better typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016, internally grounded capacity) or as a Quality (BFO_0000019)? In Spinoza perception/knowledge is an active capacity, suggesting Disposition, but this is worth confirming.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that knowledge or perception in humans occurs in exactly four kinds or ways — a core Spinozistic epistemic claim from the TIE and/or Short Treatise. I mint three new classes: Human (BFO_0000040 material entity, as the bearer), KnowledgeOrPerception (BFO_0000016 Disposition, since it is a capacity internally grounded in the human intellect), and KnowledgeKind (a subclass of KnowledgeOrPerception to serve as the genus for the four specific kinds). The four specific kinds are not yet minted because the utterance does not enumerate them and their exact source/formulation is unclear; this is flagged as an open question. KnowledgeOrPerception inheres in Human via RO_0000052. I also link KnowledgeKind as a subclass of KnowledgeOrPerception. The existing Intellect class in the ontology could refine the bearer, which is also flagged.

proposal.utterance: The Will is not free but determined by external causes.

entities.label: Will
entities.rationale: In Spinoza's system the will (voluntas) is a faculty or disposition of the mind — a capacity for striving or volition — best typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) that inheres in a mind/intellect bearer.

entities.label: FreeWillDisposition
entities.rationale: The claim that the Will is NOT free requires representing 'free will' as a disposition-type that Spinoza denies the will bears. Modeled as a subclass of Will so we can assert its non-instantiation.

entities.label: WillDetermination
entities.rationale: The positive claim: the will is determined (i.e., it has a disposition of being-determined-by-external-causes). This disposition is the complement of freedom.

entities.label: ExternalCausalDetermination
entities.rationale: The process by which external causes determine the will. Typed as a Process, subclass of the already-existing DeterminingRelation process class.

entities.label: ExternalCause
entities.rationale: An external cause in Spinoza is a causal relation originating outside the thing being determined; modeled as a specifically dependent continuant (a relation-like property) inhering in the determining entity. Alternatively could be a Role; see open_questions.

relations.rationale: WillDetermination is a species of Will — it is the determined (non-free) mode of the will.
FreeWillDisposition is a species of Will — the putative free mode that Spinoza denies.
ExternalCausalDetermination is a DeterminingRelation whose determining participants are external to the bearer of the will.
The ExternalCausalDetermination process has the WillDetermination disposition as a participant (it is the process that realizes the determined character of the will).

proposal.utterance: The soul is the idea of a certain thing in the thinking being.

entities.label: Soul
entities.rationale: In Spinoza's framework the soul (mind) is treated as a thing that persists and has an identity; within BFO the safest top-level anchor is independent continuant, paralleling the existing Intellect and Imagination classes typed as BFO_0000004. An alternative would be to type Soul as a generically dependent continuant (as an idea-pattern), but Spinoza treats it as a concrete mental individual, not merely an abstract content.

entities.label: IdeaOfAThing
entities.rationale: The soul is constituted by an idea — a representational content — about a particular thing. This is a subclass of the existing Idea class (already typed BFO_0000031). It narrows Idea to those ideas that represent (are of) a specific thing.

entities.label: ThinkingBeing
entities.rationale: The utterance refers to 'the thinking being' as the bearer in which the idea (soul) inheres or exists. This is a distinct ontological role-bearer class; it parallels Intellect and Imagination as independent continuants that are loci of mental content.

entities.label: SoulConstitutionRelation
entities.rationale: The identity claim 'soul IS the idea of a certain thing' can be read as a constitution or realisation relation that unfolds in the thinking being. Modelled as a process subclass to capture that the soul's being an idea is a dynamic, ongoing relationship rather than a static quality.

relations.rationale: Spinoza's definition equates the soul with the idea of a certain thing: Soul is defined as (is a subclass of) IdeaOfAThing. This captures the definitional identity.
IdeaOfAThing is a specialisation of the existing Idea class.
The idea (soul) inheres in the thinking being — using RO_0000052 (inheres in) to express that the soul as a dependent content is grounded in the thinking being as its bearer.
Inverse: the thinking being bears the soul (its idea-of-a-thing).

proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts Spinoza's definition of the soul as the idea of a certain thing existing in a thinking being. Four new entities are proposed: (1) Soul as an independent continuant class (aligned with Intellect and Imagination already in the ontology), (2) IdeaOfAThing as a subclass of the existing Idea class (BFO_0000031, GDC) to capture the representational content, (3) ThinkingBeing as the independent continuant bearer in which this idea inheres, and (4) SoulConstitutionRelation as an optional process capturing the ongoing identity relation. The core ontological move is the subClassOf link Soul ⊆ IdeaOfAThing and the inheres-in relation to ThinkingBeing. The most pressing open question is whether Soul should be typed as GDC rather than IC, since Spinoza treats ideas as a mode of Thought — potentially better modelled as dependent on their bearer — but the existing pattern in this ontology (Intellect, Imagination as BFO_0000004) suggests IC is the local convention.

proposal.utterance: The more essence a thing has, the more it has of action and the less of passion.

entities.label: EssenceDegree
entities.rationale: The degree or amount of essence a thing possesses is a measurable quality inhering in that thing. Spinoza treats essence as something things can have more or less of, making it a quality.

entities.label: ActionDegree
entities.rationale: The degree of action (activity, being active) a thing possesses is a measurable quality; Spinoza treats acting and suffering as polar qualities admitting of degree.

entities.label: PassionDegree
entities.rationale: The degree of passion (passivity, being acted upon) a thing possesses is a measurable quality complementary to ActionDegree.

entities.label: EssenceActionCovariance
entities.rationale: The propositional content asserting that essence degree covaries positively with action degree and negatively with passion degree is an information content entity (generically dependent continuant) — it is the Spinozistic principle being encoded.

relations.rationale: This principle is part of the content of The Ethics.

entities.label: Passion
entities.rationale: In Spinoza's framework, a passion (passio) is an affection of the mind/body whose adequate cause lies outside the bearer — it is a specifically dependent state (affect) inhering in a subject. entities.rationale: The coming-about of a passion is a process in which ExternalCausation is realized and Passion is produced. Needed to connect the disposition to its realization and to the resulting passion-state.

entities.rationale: A quality that characterizes a Passion as having an external (rather than internal) adequate cause — Spinoza's definitional mark of passion versus action.

proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance expresses a Spinozistic metaphysical axiom (Ethics I, Axiom 5 in standard editions): things not produced by an external cause share no nature with that cause. Ontologically this involves (1) a class of external-causal production processes (ExternalCausalProduction, a BFO Process), (2) a quality class for shared nature (CommonNatureQuality, a BFO Quality), (3) its negation subtype (AbsenceOfCommonNature), and (4) an individual propositional content (NoCausalCommonNatureAxiom, a generically dependent continuant) that is part of TheEthics. The axiom is the informational content; the quality classes are the ontological furniture it quantifies over. The relation between AbsenceOfCommonNature and external-cause-non-production is a constraint best expressed via a rule or annotation rather than a BFO relation, since BFO does not natively represent absence or negation — this is flagged as an open question.

proposal.utterance: The effect of an immanent cause cannot change or perish while the cause endures.

entities.label: ImmanentCausalPersistenceConstraint
entities.rationale: The claim that an effect of an immanent cause cannot change or perish while the cause endures is best captured as a disposition (internally grounded tendency) of immanent causal relationships — specifically, the dispositional constraint that grounds the persistence of effects relative to their immanent cause. It is a Disposition (BFO_0000016) because it is an internally grounded capacity/constraint of the causal structure itself.

entities.label: EffectPersistenceQuality
entities.rationale: The persistence of the effect (its not perishing or changing) while the immanent cause endures is a measurable quality of the effect-entity: its endurance is a quality that inheres in it as long as the cause remains.

entities.label: ImmanentCausalPersistence
entities.rationale: This proposition — 'the effect of an immanent cause cannot change or perish while the cause endures' — is a specific propositional content (information content entity) asserted by Spinoza. As a propositional claim it is a generically dependent continuant (information/pattern that can be copied and encoded). It is an individual because it is a specific philosophical thesis.

relations.rationale: ImmanentCausalPersistenceConstraint is a subclass of Disposition (BFO_0000016), representing the dispositional grounding of why effects cannot change or perish while their immanent cause endures.
EffectPersistenceQuality is a subclass of Quality (BFO_0000019), representing the quality of endurance that inheres in effects of immanent causes.
The specific propositional content asserting immanent causal persistence is a generically dependent continuant (information content entity).
This proposition is part of the content of The Ethics, Spinoza's primary philosophical work already in the ontology.

The ImmanentCausalPersistenceConstraint is most directly linked to God's role as immanent cause (already modeled); the constraint is realized in the process of God causing all things. This reuses existing individuals rather than minting new process instances.

The constraint that effects share persistence with their immanent cause is a species of the SameNatureConstraint already in the ontology, which captures Spinoza's principle that immanent cause and effect share the same nature.

open_questions: Should 'ImmanentCausalPersistenceConstraint' be modeled as a subclass of 'CausaSui' or 'SameNatureConstraint' rather than a direct subclass of BFO_0000016, given that in Spinoza this constraint flows from God's nature as causa sui and immanent cause?

Should 'EffectPersistenceQuality' be explicitly linked to 'ModeInstance' or 'FiniteSingularThing' as its intended bearers?
Is this proposition from a specific Part/Proposition of the Ethics (e.g., E1P24Cor or E1P28)? If so, should we create a more specific individual for that proposition?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a Spinozistic metaphysical claim: the effect of an immanent cause cannot change or perish while the cause endures. This is ontologically multi-layered. First, it encodes a propositional content (a specific thesis within The Ethics), modeled as a new individual 'ImmanentCausalPersistence' of type BFO_0000031 (generically dependent continuant), as part of the existing individual TheEthics. Second, it describes a dispositional constraint on immanent causal relations — modeled as a new class 'ImmanentCausalPersistenceConstraint' (Disposition, BFO_0000016), typed as a subclass of the existing 'SameNatureConstraint' since the persistence constraint flows from the shared nature of immanent cause and effect. Third, the persistence of the effect is a quality inhering in the effect, captured as a new class 'EffectPersistenceQuality' (Quality, BFO_0000019). Existing individuals GodImmanentCauseRole and GodCausesAllThingsProcess are linked where appropriate to avoid redundancy. entities.rationale: The infinite action of God's essence is a specific quality inhering in God (the substance individual). It is a measurable/characterizing property, fitting Quality (BFO_0000019). Modeled as an individual quality instance inhering in God.

entities.label: DenialOfPassion
entities.rationale: The denial of any passion (complete absence of passion/passivity) in God's essence is a quality inhering in God. In Spinoza, God/Substance acts from its own nature alone and cannot be affected by external causes, so this impassibility is a quality of the divine substance.

proposal.utterance: Things knowable are infinite in number.

entities.label: InfinityOfKnowableThings
entities.rationale: The infinitude of knowable things is best modeled as a quality (a measurable, specific property) inhering in the totality of knowable things or in Substance/God. It is an individual quality instance, parallel to AbsoluteInfinity already in the ontology.

entities.label: KnowableThing
entities.rationale: Knowable things, in Spinoza's framework, are objects representable by ideas (generically dependent continuants). 'KnowableThing' as a class captures the range of objects accessible to the intellect. Subclassing under Idea is appropriate since in Spinoza's system to be knowable is to be representable as an idea in the infinite intellect.

entities.label: InfiniteKnowabilityDisposition
entities.rationale: The claim that things knowable are infinite in number entails a disposition of the intellect (or of Substance) to know infinitely many things. This disposition is internally grounded in the nature of the infinite intellect.

relations.rationale: The infinity of knowable things is a divine attribute (a quality inhering in God/Substance) in Spinoza's system.
This quality of infinite knowability inheres in God as the unique infinite Substance whose intellect encompasses all knowable things.
The infinite capacity to know is an innate disposition of the true intellect, grounded internally in its nature.
The disposition to know infinitely many things inheres in the TrueIntellect individual already in the ontology.

open_questions: Is 'things knowable' here restricted to ideas in the infinite intellect (Spinoza's own usage in TIE or Ethics), or does it refer more broadly to all possible objects of knowledge including finite modes?

Should KnowableThing be typed as BFO_0000031 (generically dependent continuant / idea-content) or as BFO_0000004 (independent continuant), given that in Spinoza's system modes of Extension are also knowable?

proposal.utterance: A finite intellect cannot comprehend the infinite.

entities.label: FiniteIntellect
entities.rationale: A finite intellect is a subtype of Intellect (already existing class under BFO_0000004) distinguished by its finitude. It is a kind of independent continuant that can bear cognizers.

entities.label: InfiniteComprehensionDisposition

proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a structural limitation: finite intellects, by their finitude, cannot comprehend the infinite. proposal.utterance: A finite intellect cannot understand anything without external determination.

entities.label: FiniteIntellect
entities.rationale: A finite intellect is a kind of Intellect (already in ontology) that is also a FiniteSingularThing. It is a class of independent continuants that bear the Finitude quality and lack the capacity for self-determination.

entities.label: ExternalDetermination
entities.rationale: External determination is the disposition or capacity of a finite intellect to have its cognitive acts triggered/caused by something outside itself. It is internally grounded in the finite intellect as a necessary condition for its activity — modelling it as a Disposition (rather than a Role) because it is intrinsic to finite cognition.

entities.label: FiniteIntellectUnderstandingProcess
entities.rationale: The act of understanding by a finite intellect is a process; the claim is that every such process requires external determination to occur — linking this process class to ExternalDetermination via realization.

entities.label: ExternalDeterminationRequirement
entities.rationale: The quality that a finite intellect necessarily requires external determination to understand anything — a constraint quality inhering in every instance of FiniteIntellect, capturing the modal claim 'cannot understand without external determination'.

relations.rationale: FiniteIntellect is a subclass of Intellect already in the ontology.
A finite intellect is also a FiniteSingularThing per Spinoza's framework — it is finite and has a determinate existence.
External determination inheres in (is borne by) instances of FiniteIntellect — it is their disposition to require outside causes.
The disposition ExternalDetermination is realized in FiniteIntellectUnderstandingProcess — the understanding process is where the external determination manifests.
The quality of requiring external determination inheres in every FiniteIntellect, encoding the necessity claim.
Instances of FiniteIntellect participate in FiniteIntellectUnderstandingProcess — reversed: the process has the finite intellect as participant.

open_questions: Should FiniteIntellect be treated as a class only, or should we also create an individual (e.g., a representative finite intellect) for use in further propositions?

Is 'external determination' here specifically DeterminingRelation (already in the ontology as a Process subclass), or is it a distinct disposition inhering in the finite intellect? The existing working:DeterminingRelation is typed as BFO_0000015 (Process); if ExternalDetermination should reuse that, we can relate them instead of minting a new class.

Does this claim apply universally to ALL finite intellects (i.e., it is a necessary feature of the class), or only contingently to some? This affects whether ExternalDeterminationRequirement is an essential quality or a role.
Should FiniteIntellect be distinct from working:TrueIntellect, which is already an individual? Does TrueIntellect represent an infinite intellect in Spinoza's framework?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a modal claim: every finite intellect, whenever it engages in understanding, must be externally determined to do so — it cannot self-initiate cognition. Ontologically this commits us to (1) a class FiniteIntellect as a subclass of Intellect and FiniteSingularThing; (2) ExternalDetermination as a Disposition inhering in every FiniteIntellect, realized in acts of understanding; (3) FiniteIntellectUnderstandingProcess as the Process class in which that disposition is realized; and (4) ExternalDeterminationRequirement as a Quality encoding the necessity constraint. The existing working:DeterminingRelation is typed as a Process and could be related to ExternalDetermination, but I have kept them distinct pending clarification. The relation between ExternalDetermination (Disposition) and FiniteIntellectUnderstandingProcess (Process) uses BFO_0000054 (realized in), which is the standard BFO link between dispositions and the processes in which they manifest.

proposal.utterance: Man has an idea of God.

entities.label: Man
entities.rationale: In Spinoza's system 'Man' is a kind of finite singular thing (a material being), not a specific named individual. Modeled as a class subsuming human beings as material entities.

entities.label: IdeaOfGod
entities.rationale: The idea of God is a specific information-bearing pattern (an Idea) that can be instantiated in a human intellect; generically dependent continuant following the existing Idea class. Modeled as an individual since Spinoza asserts a singular 'idea of God' that man possesses.

entities.label: ManHasIdeaOfGodDisposition
entities.rationale: The claim that man 'has' an idea of God in Spinoza is best read as a capacity or disposition inhering in Man (the intellect), since the idea of God is available to man through reason. Modeled as a subclass of InnateCapacity (itself a Disposition).

relations.rationale: Man is a kind of finite singular thing in Spinoza's ontology; FiniteSingularThing already exists as a class.
The idea of God is an instance of the Idea class (generically dependent continuant).
The capacity to have an idea of God is an innate capacity of the intellect in Spinoza.
The disposition to have the idea of God is realized in an idea-formation process (realized in IdeaFormationProcess class).
Man is a material entity per BFO.

open_questions: Should 'Man' be an individual (e.g., a generic human representative) or remain a class (the kind Human Being)? In Spinoza's Ethics, 'Man' often functions as a type.

Is the 'idea of God' in Man innate (present by nature of the intellect) or acquired through reasoning? This affects whether ManHasIdeaOfGodDisposition should be typed as InnateCapacity or another disposition.

Should IdeaOfGod be related to the existing individual 'God' via a specific relation (e.g., 'is about', 'represents')? BFO itself lacks an 'aboutness' relation, but we could use an annotation property or mint a working:isAbout relation.
Does the statement assert that every instance of Man bears this disposition, or only that some man does? This affects whether we axiomatize this as a universal restriction on the Man class.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'Man has an idea of God' asserts three things: (1) there is a kind of entity, Man, that is a finite material being; (2) there is an informational object, the idea of God, which is a generically dependent continuant (an Idea); and (3) Man bears a disposition or capacity to possess this idea. I model Man as a new class (subclass of FiniteSingularThing and BFO material entity), IdeaOfGod as an individual of the existing Idea class, and ManHasIdeaOfGodDisposition as a new disposition class (subclass of InnateCapacity) that inheres in Man and is realized in IdeaFormationProcess. Several interpretive questions remain open, notably whether the 'having' of the idea is innate or rational, and how to represent the intentional 'aboutness' relation between the idea and God.

relations.rationale: FormalExistenceInNature is a subclass of Quality, since it is a mode of being of substances in Nature.
ObjectiveExistenceInIntellect is a subclass of Quality, characterizing existence as represented in an intellect.
The entailment process is a subclass of Process.
The individual disposition of God's intellect to contain all substances is an instance of Disposition.
God (as Substance individual) bears the disposition of having all substances exist in its intellect and thereby formally in Nature.
The disposition is realized in the entailment process by which substances known in God's intellect come to exist formally in Nature.
The formal existence entailment process is a species of DeterminingRelation, since God's intellect determines the formal existence of substances in Nature.

open_questions: Is 'God's intellect' here identical to the individual TrueIntellect already in the ontology, or is it a distinct individual (i.e., God's own intellect as an attribute or mode)?

Should ObjectiveExistenceInIntellect be modeled as inhering in the Substance (as how the substance is known) or in the Intellect (as the content of an intellectual state)? The BFO typing may shift depending on the answer.
Does 'exists formally in Nature' mean every substance is a part of WholeOfNature, warranting a BFO_0000050 (part of) relation from Substance to WholeOfNature?

Is the entailment direction: (1) God's intellect contains exactly those substances that exist formally in Nature (co-extensionality), or (2) God's intellect is a sufficient condition for formal existence (one-directional necessitation)? This affects whether we need a biconditional or a unidirectional relation.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a necessitation relation between two modes of existence Spinoza distinguishes: objective existence (being in an intellect) and formal existence (being as a concrete thing in Nature). I mint two Quality subclasses (ObjectiveExistenceInIntellect, FormalExistenceInNature) to represent these two modes as qualities that substances bear, a Process class (FormalExistenceEntailmentProcess) to represent the entailment or necessitation by which the former grounds the latter, and an individual Disposition (GodIntellectContainsSubstancesDisposition) inhering in God (the existing individual) to capture that God's intellect is the epistemic ground for all substances existing formally in Nature. I link the disposition to the process via BFO_0000054 (realized in) and classify the process as a DeterminingRelation (already in the ontology). Several interpretive questions remain open about the direction of entailment and the identity of 'God's intellect'.

proposal.utterance: A substance cannot limit itself through its own will.

entities.label: SelfLimitationByWill
entities.rationale: The capacity for a substance to limit itself through its own will is a putative disposition; the claim is that this disposition is absent in / incompatible with Substance. Modeling it as a Disposition class allows us to assert its non-instantiation in Substance.

entities.label: WillOfSubstance
entities.rationale: The concept of a substance having a 'will' that could act upon itself is itself a disposition-like capacity being denied here. Modeling it as a class of Disposition allows the denial (absence) to be expressed as a quality or constraint.

entities.label: AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWill
entities.rationale: The denial that a substance can limit itself through its own will is best expressed as a quality inhering in Substance — the absence of the self-limitation-by-will disposition. This parallels existing individuals like AbsenceOfContingency.

entities.label: AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWillInstance
entities.rationale: An individual instance of the absence-of-self-limitation quality inhering in the Substance individual (God/WholeOfNature), asserting the specific ontological commitment made by this utterance.

relations.rationale: AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWill is a subclass of Quality, parallel to AbsenceOfContingency.
SelfLimitationByWill is a subclass of Disposition, representing the capacity being denied.
WillOfSubstance is a subclass of Disposition, modeling the putative volition of a substance.
The individual is typed as an instance of the absence quality class.
This quality inheres in God (the unique Substance individual), asserting the claim that Substance cannot limit itself by will.

open_questions: Is 'will' (voluntas) here meant as an anthropomorphic attribution being denied, or as a technical Spinozistic concept (e.g., conatus or intellect)? This affects whether WillOfSubstance should be linked to existing conatus/intellect individuals.
Should AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWillInstance also inhere in WholeOfNature, since God and WholeOfNature are treated as co-extensive in this ontology?
Is this claim derived from a specific proposition in the Ethics (e.g., Ethics I, Prop. 17, Cor. 2 denying intellect and will to God)? If so, should we link it to TheEthics individual as its source?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a negative ontological claim: that Substance lacks the disposition to limit itself through its own will. Following the pattern of existing individuals like AbsenceOfContingency, I model this as a Quality class (AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWill) with an individual instance inhering in God (the Substance individual). I also mint SelfLimitationByWill and WillOfSubstance as Disposition classes to represent the capacities being denied, enabling future reasoning about their incompatibility with Substance. The core relation asserted is that AbsenceOfSelfLimitationByWillInstance inheres in (RO_0000052) the individual God. This is consistent with Spinoza's Ethics I, where God is not determined by will or intellect but acts solely from the necessity of its own nature — a claim that aligns with the existing CausaSui and ExistenceNecessitation dispositions already in the ontology.

proposal.utterance: Any limited substance is limited by its cause, which is God.

entities.label: LimitedByExternalCause
entities.rationale: The property of being limited by an external cause is an internally-grounded disposition of limited (finite) substances; it captures the structural fact that any substance that is not absolute has its limitation grounded in a cause outside itself.

entities.label: CausalLimitationByGod
entities.rationale: The process by which God (as immanent, first cause) determines and thereby limits a finite/limited substance. This is a sub-type of DeterminingRelation already in the ontology.

entities.label: LimitedSubstance
entities.rationale: A limited/finite substance is a sub-type of Substance (already in the ontology). It is distinct from the infinite, self-caused Substance (God). Relates to existing FiniteSingularThing but at the level of substance rather than mode.

relations.rationale: A limited substance is a kind of Substance in Spinoza's framework, but one that does not self-cause its existence.
A limited substance is also a finite singular thing; both classes apply simultaneously under BFO's independent continuant hierarchy.
LimitedByExternalCause is a disposition inhering in limited substances.
CausalLimitationByGod is a specific kind of DeterminingRelation (already in ontology) in which God is the determining cause.
The disposition of being limited by an external cause is realized in the process of God causally limiting the substance.
God participates in (as the cause) every process of causal limitation of limited substances.
The limited substance participates in the process of being limited by its cause (God).

God's disposition to cause all things (already in ontology as GodCausesAllThings individual) entails the disposition that limits limited substances; the limitation disposition is a specific expression of GodCausesAllThings.

open_questions: Should 'LimitedSubstance' be treated as identical to 'FiniteSingularThing' (already in the ontology), or does the utterance specifically intend a substance-level (not mode-level) entity distinct from FiniteSingularThing?

Spinoza's mature view in the Ethics is that there is only one Substance (God/Nature), and what we might call 'limited substances' are actually modes. Does this utterance reflect an earlier, less settled view (e.g., Short Treatise) where finite substances are admitted, or should 'LimitedSubstance' be re-typed as a Mode?
Should CausalLimitationByGod be linked to GodImmanentCauseRole (already in ontology) to express that God limits things as immanent, not transitive, cause?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that any limited (finite) substance has its limitation grounded in a cause external to itself, and that cause is God. This introduces three new ontological items: (1) a class LimitedSubstance (subclass of Substance and FiniteSingularThing) representing substances that are not self-caused; (2) a disposition class LimitedByExternalCause inhering in such substances, capturing the structural property of being causally dependent on another; and (3) a process class CausalLimitationByGod (subclass of the existing DeterminingRelation) by which God determines and thereby limits finite substances. The disposition is realized in that process, and both God and the LimitedSubstance participate in it. The individual God (already in the ontology) is asserted as participant/cause in every such process. An important open question is whether Spinoza here means substances in a strict sense or (as the Ethics ultimately concludes) that all finite things are modes of the one infinite Substance—which would suggest LimitedSubstance should be re-typed as a subclass of Mode rather than Substance.

proposal.utterance: God is omnipotent.

entities.label: OmnipotenceOfGod
entities.rationale: Omnipotence is a quality (a divine attribute) inhering in God as its bearer. It is a specifically dependent continuant of type Quality, consistent with existing DivineAttribute subclass of BFO_0000019.

relations.rationale: Omnipotence is an instance of DivineAttribute (a subclass of Quality, BFO_0000019).
The quality OmnipotenceOfGod inheres in the individual God, per BFO's inheres-in relation for specifically dependent continuants.
God bears the quality OmnipotenceOfGod; inverse of inheres-in.

open_questions: In Spinoza's system, 'omnipotence' is typically identified with God's infinite power (potentia) to exist and act, closely related to CausaSui and ExistenceNecessitation already in the ontology. Should OmnipotenceOfGod be linked to or equated with any of those existing individuals (e.g., GodCausesAllThings, NecessaryExistenceOfGod)?
Should OmnipotenceOfGod also be typed as an instance of EssentialExistenceQuality or a new subclass of DivineAttribute (e.g., OmnipotenceQuality) to support reasoning over multiple divine attributes?
proposal.rationale_summary: The statement 'God is omnipotent' asserts that omnipotence is a property of God. In BFO terms this is best modeled as a Quality (specifically dependent continuant) inhering in the individual God. The existing class DivineAttribute (subclass of BFO_0000019 Quality) is the appropriate type for such divine qualities. A new individual OmnipotenceOfGod is minted as an instance of DivineAttribute, with inheres-in and bearer-of relations connecting it to the existing God individual. No new classes are needed. Open questions flag whether this should be linked to related Spinozistic notions already in the ontology (CausaSui, ExistenceNecessitation, GodCausesAllThings) since for Spinoza omnipotence is not a separate attribute but follows from God's nature as causa sui.

proposal.utterance: God is all goodness and fullness.

entities.label: DivineGoodnessQuality
entities.rationale: Goodness predicated of God is a quality inhering in the God individual, typed as Quality (BFO_0000019) and an instance of DivineAttribute.

entities.label: DivineFullnessQuality
entities.rationale: Fullness predicated of God is a quality inhering in the God individual, typed as Quality (BFO_0000019) and an instance of DivineAttribute. 'Fullness' (plenitudo) connotes the complete positive reality of God's essence.

relations.rationale: Goodness is a divine attribute quality, an instance of the DivineAttribute class.
The quality of goodness inheres in God as its bearer.
God bears the quality of goodness.
Fullness is a divine attribute quality, an instance of the DivineAttribute class.
The quality of fullness inheres in God as its bearer.
God bears the quality of fullness.

open_questions: In Spinoza's framework, 'goodness' is not straightforwardly predicated of God as a moral attribute (Ethics Part I rejects anthropomorphic predicates). Does this utterance reflect a non-Spinozistic theological claim (e.g., from Scholastic or traditional theism) rather than Spinoza's own position? If so, should these qualities be tagged as belonging to a different doctrinal context?

Is 'fullness' meant in the Scholastic sense of 'plenitudo essendi' (complete positive being, ens realissimum), or in a different sense? This affects whether it overlaps with AbsoluteInfinity or EssentialExistenceQuality already in the ontology.
Should DivineGoodnessQuality be related to or subsumed under AbsoluteInfinity or EssentialExistenceQuality, given that those individuals are already in the graph as qualities of God?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance predicates two qualities—goodness and fullness—of God. Under BFO, qualities inhere in their bearer, so both are modeled as individual instances of Quality (BFO_0000019) and specifically as instances of the existing DivineAttribute class, with RO_0000052 (inheres in) linking them to the God individual and RO_0000053 (bearer of) linking God to them. Notably, Spinoza himself is ambivalent about predicating 'goodness' of God in the Ethics (he rejects teleological and moral attributes of Substance), so this may represent a non-Spinozistic or Scholastic theological claim; this tension is flagged in open questions. 'Fullness' is tentatively modeled as a distinct quality from AbsoluteInfinity and EssentialExistenceQuality already present, but the user should clarify whether consolidation is appropriate.

proposal.utterance: Every substance is perfect in its kind.

entities.label: SubstancePerfection
entities.rationale: Perfection-in-kind is a quality that inheres in each substance; in Spinoza's system, a substance's perfection is a measurable property of its being, grounded in its essence. Modeled as a subclass of Quality (BFO_0000019).

entities.label: SubstancePerfectionInKindQuality
entities.rationale: More specific class capturing 'perfect in its kind' — perfection relative to the kind/attribute of the substance. This is distinct from absolute divine perfection and grounds the claim that every substance is fully what it is within its own attribute-kind.

relations.rationale: SubstancePerfection is a quality inhering in substances.
Perfection-in-kind is a more specific form of substance perfection.
Perfection in kind is an attribute-level quality of substance, aligning with the existing AttributeOfSubstance class in the ontology.

The universal claim 'every substance is perfect in its kind' should be encoded as a subClassOf restriction: Substance rdfs:subClassOf (bearer of some SubstancePerfectionInKindQuality). This is noted as an OWL restriction to be elaborated — flagged in open_questions.

open_questions: Should 'perfect in its kind' be encoded as a universal restriction on Substance (i.e., every instance of Substance must bear an instance of SubstancePerfectionInKindQuality), expressed as an OWL existential/universal restriction? If so, do you want the reasoner to enforce this as a necessary condition on Substance?

Does 'perfection in kind' here refer to the Spinozistic sense that a thing fully expresses its essence within its attribute (so each substance is the fullest expression of its kind), or a more evaluative sense of moral/axiological perfection? proposal.utterance: Everything that exists in God's intellect exists formally in Nature.

entities.label: FormalExistenceInNature
entities.rationale: The formal existence of something in Nature is a quality that inheres in entities that are instantiated (formally existing) within the totality of Nature. entities.label: IntellectToNatureCorrespondenceDisposition
entities.rationale: The general disposition of God/Nature by which whatever is contained in the divine intellect is disposed to be formally instantiated in Nature. This captures the structural/metaphysical principle asserted by the utterance as an internally-grounded capacity of God or Nature.

entities.label: IntellectToNatureCorrespondencePrinciple
entities.rationale: The principle itself—'Whatever is in God's intellect exists formally in Nature'—is an informational/propositional content that can be represented and copied; it is a generically dependent continuant, specifically a philosophical doctrine.

entities.label: GodIntellect
entities.rationale: God's intellect as a specific individual intellect (a part of God as substance). The existing class Intellect (parent BFO_0000004) covers this; GodIntellect is the individual divine intellect referenced in the utterance.

proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts Spinoza's doctrine that whatever exists in God's intellect (objectively/representationally) also exists formally (actually) in Nature. proposal.utterance: Extension is infinite by nature.

entities.label: Extension
entities.rationale: In Spinoza's system, Extension (Extensio) is one of the infinite attributes of God/Substance, perceived by intellect as constituting God's essence. As an attribute it is a quality-like entity inhering in Substance. Modeling it as a subclass of DivineAttribute (which is already a subclass of BFO Quality) captures this. It is a class because multiple modal expressions can be instances of it.

entities.label: InfiniteByNatureQuality
entities.rationale: The predicate 'infinite by nature' expresses a quality of Extension: it is infinite not contingently but by its own nature (i.e., qua attribute of the one infinite Substance). This is a Quality class distinct from AbsoluteInfinity (which is an individual quality of God as a whole). Note: could alternatively be modeled as a disposition; flagged in open_questions.

relations.rationale: Extension is an infinite attribute of God/Substance, so it falls under the existing DivineAttribute class.

The utterance asserts that Extension is infinite by nature; modeling this as a subclass relationship means every instance of Extension bears InfiniteByNatureQuality, capturing the universal necessity of this property for Extension.

open_questions: Should 'infinite by nature' be modeled as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) rather than a Quality (BFO_0000019)? A Disposition would stress that Extension is disposed to be infinite by its intrinsic nature, whereas a Quality stresses it as a static property. Which fits Spinoza's intent better here?

Is Extension being introduced as a class (covering all modal expressions under the attribute) or as an individual attribute-instance of God analogous to AbsoluteInfinity? If there is exactly one Extension (monism), it may warrant individual status.
Should Extension be linked directly to the individual God via RO_0000052 (inheres in) if treated as an individual quality/attribute?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'Extension is infinite by nature' introduces two ontological commitments in Spinoza's metaphysics: (1) Extension as one of the infinite attributes of God/Substance, and (2) the predicate 'infinite by nature' as a quality or disposition that belongs to Extension essentially. I model Extension as a new class under the existing DivineAttribute class (itself under BFO Quality), since attributes in Spinoza are what the intellect perceives as constituting the essence of Substance and can be thought of as quality-universals. I introduce InfiniteByNatureQuality as a new Quality class to capture the 'by nature' (i.e., essentially, not contingently) infinite character of Extension, and link Extension to it via subClassOf so that any instance of Extension necessarily bears this quality. The existing AbsoluteInfinity individual (a quality of God overall) is related but distinct, as InfiniteByNatureQuality is the attribute-level infinite character. Key open questions remain about whether individual vs. class modeling is preferable for Extension given Spinoza's monism.

proposal.utterance: Division occurs only in modes of substance, never in substance itself.

entities.label: DivisionConstraint
entities.rationale: The impossibility of division in substance is an internally grounded constraint — a disposition (specifically a negative one: the incapacity to be divided). This is best typed as a Disposition subclass under BFO_0000016.

entities.label: DivisibilityOfMode
entities.rationale: Divisibility, as a capacity that inheres in modes (not in substance), is an internally grounded disposition of modes. Distinct from DivisionConstraint which applies to Substance.

entities.label: IndivisibilityOfSubstance
entities.rationale: Indivisibility is a quality of Substance — a property that can be predicated of it as a measurable/characterizing attribute. It is distinct from the disposition to resist division; it is a standing characteristic.

relations.rationale: Indivisibility is an attribute (quality) that characterizes Substance, placing it under the existing AttributeOfSubstance quality class.

DivisionConstraint (the incapacity for division) is a constraint disposition that applies to Substance, consistent with SubstanceProductionConstraint as a parent. Alternatively it could stand alone; flagged in open_questions.
DivisibilityOfMode inheres in modes (instances of working:Mode), grounding the capacity for division at the level of modes only.
DivisionConstraint is typed as a disposition (BFO_0000016) that inheres in Substance.

open_questions: Should DivisionConstraint be a subclass of SubstanceProductionConstraint (which concerns production/causal constraints on Substance), or should it be an independent disposition class directly under BFO_0000016? The latter may be cleaner since indivisibility is not primarily a production constraint.

Is IndivisibilityOfSubstance better modeled as a Quality (BFO_0000019) or as a negative Disposition (BFO_0000016, i.e., an incapacity)? Spinoza's text treats it as a property of Substance's nature, which suggests Quality, but the modal/logical character could favour Disposition.
Should we assert an individual IndivisibilityOfSubstance quality inhering in the God individual (since God = Substance in the ontology), or is a class-level assertion sufficient at this stage?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts two complementary Spinozist claims: (1) Substance cannot be divided — indivisibility is an essential quality of Substance; and (2) division is possible only at the level of modes of Substance. To capture this I mint three new entities: IndivisibilityOfSubstance as a Quality (BFO_0000019) subclassing the existing AttributeOfSubstance, because indivisibility is a standing characteristic of Substance; DivisionConstraint as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) representing the internally grounded incapacity of Substance to be divided; and DivisibilityOfMode as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) representing the capacity for division that inheres specifically in modes. The relation between DivisionConstraint and the existing SubstanceProductionConstraint is uncertain and flagged. No new individuals are introduced; the class-level commitments suffice to encode the ontological claim.
